intro: You're looking for a construction insurance broker near you, which usually means you run a building or trades business and want cover that actually fits the work you do. Perhaps a contract has landed and you need to show the right insurance before you start, or your current policy doesn't reflect the plant you hire or the projects you take on. A broker can talk through what you need and go to insurers on your behalf.
need_heading: What people searching for a construction insurance broker usually need
need_lead: Construction work brings risks that a standard trades policy may not fully cover, and a broker helps you work out what fits.
needs: You've been asked for public liability cover at a particular limit before a contract can start, and you need a policy that matches what the client requires.
You take on projects where contract works cover is needed to protect the build itself while it's underway.
You hire plant or equipment and want to know whether your existing cover extends to it or whether hired plant needs its own protection.
You employ people on site and need employers' liability arranged properly alongside your other construction cover.
You've had a quote but the exclusions weren't clear, and you want a broker to explain what is and isn't covered before you commit.
context_heading: Understanding how construction insurance brokers work
context: Insurance brokers and intermediaries in the UK must be authorised by the FCA, or be appointed representatives of an authorised firm, and you can check them on the FCA register. Many brokers belong to the British Insurance Brokers' Association, and some hold Chartered status from the Chartered Insurance Institute. A broker must understand your demands and needs, explain key policy features and exclusions, and tell you how they are paid.

Because construction cover spans public liability, employers' liability, contract works and plant, the right policy depends on the work you actually do and the contracts you sign. If a complaint isn't resolved, it can go to the Financial Ombudsman Service. When comparing brokers, ask what they specialise in and how they will explain exclusions, rather than assuming one is best for your situation.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the type of construction work you do, such as building, groundworks, roofing or another trade, so the broker understands your exposure.
Say whether you work as a sole trader, partnership or limited company, as this affects what cover is appropriate.
Mention any contract requirement you've been given, including the type of cover and the limit the client has asked for.
Explain whether you employ anyone on site and, if so, whether you need employers' liability cover.
List the plant and equipment you use, noting anything you hire rather than own.
Note the size and type of projects you take on, including whether contract works cover is likely to be needed.
questions_heading: Questions to ask the construction insurance broker
questions: Which insurers do you approach for construction trades, and what experience do you have with my type of work?
How will you make sure the public liability limit meets what my contract requires?
Will contract works cover be included for my projects, and what does it protect?
Does the policy cover hired plant, or will I need separate cover for equipment I hire in?
Can you explain the main exclusions that would affect a construction business like mine?
How are you paid for arranging my cover, and will you set that out in writing?

faqs.q: Do I need a broker rather than going direct to an insurer?
faqs.a: You can buy construction cover directly, but a broker can compare insurers and explain exclusions across policies. That can help when your work spans several types of cover, such as public liability, contract works and hired plant.

Contract works cover protects the project itself while it's being built, including materials and work in progress. It's often required alongside public liability on construction contracts, so it's worth checking what your contract asks for.

faqs.q: How do I check a construction insurance broker is properly authorised?
faqs.a: Insurance brokers and intermediaries in the UK must be authorised by the FCA, or be appointed representatives of an authorised firm. You can check them on the FCA register before you go ahead.

faqs.q: What if I'm unhappy with the broker's service?
faqs.a: Brokers must explain key policy features and exclusions and tell you how they are paid. If a complaint isn't resolved, it can be escalated to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

extra_heading: What 'near me' means for construction insurance
extra: Searching for a construction insurance broker near me usually means you want someone you can meet face to face or who understands the local area. But for construction cover, what really matters is whether the broker knows your trade and the type of work you do, not just how close they are. A broker further away who specialises in construction may serve you better than a local generalist.

When you contact a broker, ask how they will handle your case: will you deal with the same person throughout, and how quickly do they respond when you need to adjust cover or make a claim? These practical points often matter more than a nearby postcode. Many brokers work by phone and email, so location need not be a barrier.

extra_faqs.q: Does my construction insurance broker need to be local?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. What matters more is whether the broker understands construction risks and can arrange the cover your contracts require. Many brokers work remotely and can still provide a personal service.

extra_faqs.q: How can I compare construction insurance brokers?
extra_faqs.a: Ask each broker about their experience with your type of construction work and how they explain exclusions. Also check they are authorised by the FCA and ask how they are paid. You can then judge which broker suits you best.
